instruction: What happens when I first get to the hospital?
response: When you first arrive at Children's Hospital, you'll come in through the big main entrance in the B Tower. A friendly person at a desk might say hello! Then you and your grown-up will go up to the second floor to a place called Patient Registration. That's where they write down your name and make sure everything is ready for your visit. It's kind of like checking in at a hotel — but instead of getting a room key, you'll get a special bracelet to wear on your wrist!

instruction: What is the bracelet they put on my arm?
response: That bracelet is called an armband, and it's really important! It has your name, your birthday, a special hospital number, and a little barcode on it — kind of like the barcodes on things at the grocery store. Before anyone gives you medicine or does a test, they'll look at your bracelet to make sure they have the right person. It doesn't hurt to wear it, and it helps keep you safe the whole time you're at the hospital.

instruction: Why do they keep asking me my name and birthday?
response: Great question! The nurses and doctors ask your name and birthday a lot because they want to make really, really sure they're helping the right kid. It's one of the ways the hospital keeps you safe. Even though they already know who you are, checking is like double-checking your homework — it just makes sure everything is exactly right. So don't worry if they ask you again and again. It means they're being extra careful with you!

instruction: What does the hospital smell like?
response: The hospital has its own special smell! It's mostly from the cleaning stuff they use to keep everything super clean and germ-free. It might smell a little like hand sanitizer or soap. Some people think it smells a bit different from home, and that's totally normal. The hospital is also fragrance-free, which means nobody wears perfume or strong-smelling things, so the air stays easy to breathe for everyone.

instruction: I'm scared of needles. What will they do?
response: It's totally okay to feel scared of needles — lots of kids feel that way! The good news is that Children's Hospital has something called the Comfort Promise. That means they'll do everything they can to make needle time easier for you. They can put a special numbing cream on your skin so you barely feel anything. They'll also help you sit in a cozy position, and you can watch a video or play with a toy to keep your mind busy. You can always tell your nurse if you're feeling scared — they want to help!

instruction: What is numbing cream?
response: Numbing cream is a special cream or gel that the nurse puts on your skin before a needle poke. It makes that little spot on your skin feel kind of sleepy, so when the needle comes, you feel way less of it — or sometimes nothing at all! It's part of something called the Comfort Promise at Children's Hospital. The cream needs a little bit of time to work, so the nurse will put it on and then wait before doing the needle part.

instruction: What sounds will I hear in the hospital?
response: The hospital has lots of interesting sounds! You might hear beeping from machines that help the doctors and nurses watch over patients. You might hear people talking, shoes squeaking on the shiny floors, and sometimes a ding from an elevator. There might also be announcements on a speaker, kind of like at school. If you're near the babies' area, you might hear little babies crying. All these sounds are normal! If any sound worries you, just ask your grown-up or a nurse what it is.

instruction: What does a hospital room look like?
response: Your hospital room will have a special bed that can go up and down — which is pretty cool! There are buttons to move it. There will be a little table for your things, and rails on the side of the bed to keep you safe. You'll see a screen or monitor on the wall, and there might be some medical equipment nearby. There's also a spot where your mom, dad, or caregiver can sit or even sleep next to you. You can bring some of your favourite toys and books from home to make it feel more like your own space!

instruction: Can I bring my teddy bear to the hospital?
response: Yes, you can bring your teddy bear! Children's Hospital says you can bring a few favourite toys, books, and even family pictures to help you feel more at home. Just make sure your teddy is clean before you bring it — wipeable or washable toys are the best. The hospital asks that you don't bring too many things, and that you don't share your toys with other kids in the hospital, because that helps stop germs from spreading. But your teddy is welcome to stay right with you!

instruction: What will I eat at the hospital?
response: The hospital has food for you! Breakfast comes around 7:45 in the morning, lunch is around 11:45, and dinner comes around 4:45 in the afternoon. A menu will come on your breakfast tray so you can pick what you'd like to eat the next day — kind of like ordering from a restaurant! If you have any allergies or special foods you need, just tell your nurse and they'll make sure your meals are right for you. Your grown-up can also get food from the Tim Hortons in the hospital.

instruction: Is there a place to play at the hospital?
response: Yes! There are fun places to play. If you're a younger kid, there's a cool nature-themed playroom called Ashley's Backyard on the sixth floor. If you're a bit older, there's the School-Age Activity Room where you can do crafts, play board games, build with LEGO, and do puzzles. There's even a special room called the SMILE Room that has bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, and music — it's like a magical sensory room! Your nurse can help you find these spaces.

instruction: What is the SMILE Room?
response: The SMILE Room is one of the coolest rooms in the hospital! It's on the sixth floor in room B6-261, and it's filled with amazing sensory stuff to help you relax or have fun. There are bubble columns that light up, fibre optic lights you can touch, mirrors, and music. It's designed to help kids feel calm and comfortable. If you'd like to visit the SMILE Room, ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist — they can help you get there!

instruction: Will I have to wear a hospital gown?
response: Sometimes kids wear a hospital gown, which is a special loose shirt that the hospital gives you. It ties in the back and is really comfy and easy for the doctors and nurses to work with. But guess what — you can also wear your own pyjamas or comfy clothes from home a lot of the time! Your nurse will let you know if you need to put on a gown for something special, like a test or procedure. And don't forget to bring your own slippers or shoes too!

instruction: What is hand sanitizer and why is it everywhere?
response: You'll see little bottles and dispensers of hand sanitizer all over the hospital — they're everywhere! It's a special gel you rub on your hands to get rid of germs. The hospital calls it ABHR, which stands for alcohol-based hand rub. Everyone uses it — doctors, nurses, your family, and you too! You should clean your hands when you go into a room, when you leave a room, and before you eat. It helps keep germs from spreading so everyone stays healthier.

instruction: Why do some rooms have signs on the door?
response: Sometimes you might see a colourful sign on a door when you're walking around the hospital. Those signs are there to let people know about special rules for that room. It might mean the person inside needs extra germ protection. The sign might say that visitors need to wear gloves, a gown, or a mask before going in. If you see a sign like that, just check with a nurse before you go in. It's all about keeping everyone safe and healthy!

instruction: What is a blood pressure cuff?
response: A blood pressure cuff is like a soft, puffy armband that wraps around your arm. When the nurse turns it on, it gently squeezes your arm for a few seconds — kind of like a hug for your arm! Then it lets go. It's measuring how hard your heart is pumping blood through your body. It doesn't hurt, but the squeezing feeling might feel a little weird the first time. It only takes a minute, and then it's all done!

instruction: What is a thermometer?
response: A thermometer is a tool the nurse uses to check your temperature — that means finding out if your body is warmer than it should be. There are different kinds! Some go under your tongue, some go in your ear, and some just touch your forehead. It only takes a few seconds and doesn't hurt at all. If your body is too warm, it might mean you have a fever, and the doctors will want to know about it so they can help you feel better.

instruction: What is that clip thing they put on my finger?
response: That little clip is called a pulse oximeter, but you can think of it as a finger light! It clips gently onto your finger and shines a tiny red light through your skin. It's checking how much oxygen is in your blood — oxygen is the stuff you breathe in that your body needs. It doesn't hurt at all, and some kids think the glowing red light looks pretty cool! The nurse just needs to make sure your body is getting all the oxygen it needs.

instruction: Why is the hospital so big?
response: Children's Hospital is part of a really big place called Victoria Hospital in London, Ontario. It's big because it has lots of different areas where different kinds of care happen. The hospital uses letters and numbers to organize everything — like Zone B and Zone D. Your room number even tells you which zone and floor you're on! For example, room B2-503 means Zone B, second floor, room 503. If you ever get confused, there are helpers at the information desks and a cool app called MazeMap that works like a map for the hospital.

instruction: Who are the people in the colourful clothes?
response: Those colourful clothes are called scrubs! Lots of people at the hospital wear them — doctors, nurses, and other helpers. They're comfy and easy to keep clean. Different people might wear different colours, but everyone who takes care of you is part of your care team. If you're ever not sure who someone is, it's totally okay to ask them! They all wear name tags too, so you can see their name and what their job is.

instruction: What happens when I have to get an X-ray?
response: An X-ray is like taking a special picture of the inside of your body — how cool is that? You'll go to a special room with a big camera-like machine. The person taking the X-ray will help you get into the right position, and then they'll step behind a screen. You'll hear a little click or buzz, and that's it! It doesn't hurt at all. You just need to hold really still for a second, like you're playing freeze tag. The picture helps the doctors see your bones and make sure everything looks good inside.

instruction: What does an IV look like?
response: An IV is a tiny, thin tube that goes into a vein in your hand or arm. It's connected to a bag of clear liquid that hangs on a tall pole with wheels. The liquid slowly drips down through the tube into your body. It's how the hospital gives you water, medicine, or other things your body might need. Getting the IV put in uses a small needle, but remember — the Comfort Promise means they'll use numbing cream and help you stay comfortable. Once it's in, the needle comes out and just a soft little tube stays.

instruction: Will the IV hurt?
response: When the IV first goes in, there's a little poke from a small needle. But the good news is the nurses at Children's Hospital use the Comfort Promise! That means they can put numbing cream on your skin first so you barely feel the poke. They'll also help you sit in a cozy position, and you can watch something fun or play with a toy while it happens. Once the IV is in, the needle comes out, and the soft tube that stays doesn't hurt. If something ever feels uncomfortable, just tell your nurse right away.

instruction: What is that beeping machine next to my bed?
response: That beeping machine is called a monitor, and it's like a helper that watches over you! It keeps track of things like how fast your heart is beating and how much oxygen is in your blood. The beeping sounds usually mean everything is working fine — it's just the machine doing its job. Sometimes it beeps a little louder if something moves or gets loose, like the clip on your finger. A nurse will always come check if the beeping changes, so you don't need to worry about it!

instruction: Why do I have to stay in bed?
response: Sometimes the doctors and nurses want you to stay in bed so your body can rest and get better. It also helps them keep an eye on you and make sure all the machines and tubes are working just right. But staying in bed doesn't mean you can't have fun! You can play with toys, read books, watch shows, or do crafts right from your bed. And when it's safe, your nurse might let you get up and walk around or visit one of the playrooms.

instruction: What is the button I can press to call the nurse?
response: There's a special button near your bed called the call button. When you press it, it sends a little signal to the nurses' station so they know you need help. It's kind of like ringing a doorbell! You can press it any time you need something — if you're thirsty, if something hurts, or if you just have a question. A nurse will come to your room to see how they can help. It's there for you, so don't be shy about using it!

instruction: Why does the nurse come check on me at night?
response: Even when you're sleeping, the nurses are still looking after you! They come by your room during the night to make sure you're comfortable, safe, and doing well. They might check the machines, look at your bracelet, or just peek in to see that you're sleeping okay. They try to be really quiet so they don't wake you up. It's like having someone watch over you to make sure everything is good while you rest.

instruction: Can I watch TV in the hospital?
response: Yes, you can! Children's Hospital has a special entertainment site where you can watch Rogers TV for free. If your family has a streaming service like Netflix or Disney+, you can log in with your own account and watch your favourite shows too! There are also patient telephones you can use to call people for free if they're local or toll-free numbers. And you're welcome to use your own phone or tablet to stay connected with friends and family.

instruction: Where does my family park the car?
response: Your family will most likely park in the parking garage called Parking Lot P8. It's right near Children's Hospital and you get to it from Baseline Road. When you drive in, a machine gives you a ticket. When it's time to leave, your grown-up pays for the ticket at a machine by the elevators on the second floor of the garage. There are also other parking lots around the hospital. And don't worry — if it's hard to walk from the car, there are drop-off spots right at the entrance where someone can let you out before parking.

instruction: What happens if I get lost in the hospital?
response: The hospital is really big, but there are lots of people who can help you if you feel lost! There are information desks with friendly helpers, and there are guide volunteers wearing special outfits near the main entrances. You can also look for any hospital staff member — they all wear name tags and will be happy to help. There are also maps on the walls and special screens called wayfinding kiosks. Just remember, your room number tells you your zone and floor, like B2 means Zone B, floor 2!

instruction: Can my mom or dad sleep at the hospital with me?
response: Yes! Children's Hospital knows how important it is to have your family close by. Most rooms have a spot where your mom, dad, or caregiver can sleep right next to you. They'll get clean sheets, pillows, and blankets. But here's an important rule — you need to sleep in your own hospital bed, not with your grown-up, because the nurses need to be able to reach you easily. Your grown-up will be right beside you the whole night, though!

instruction: What is that thing on the wall that looks like a phone?
response: That's the patient telephone! You can use it to make calls to people in London or to toll-free numbers, and it's totally free. If you want to call your grandma or your best friend to tell them about your day, you can use it! Most kids also use their own cell phones, which is totally fine too. The hospital wants you to be able to stay in touch with the people you love while you're here.

instruction: What is an ultrasound?
response: An ultrasound is a way for doctors to look inside your body using sound waves — not the kind of sound you can hear, though! The person doing the ultrasound will put some warm, squishy gel on your skin and then gently move a smooth wand over it. On a screen nearby, a picture will appear showing what's inside your body. It doesn't hurt at all! The gel might feel a little cold and gooey, but you can wipe it off when it's done. It's kind of like seeing a secret picture of what's going on inside you.

instruction: What is a stethoscope?
response: A stethoscope is that thing you've probably seen doctors and nurses wear around their necks! It has two little pieces that go in their ears and a round disc they press against your chest or back. It lets them listen to your heart beating and your lungs breathing. When the disc first touches your skin, it might feel a little cold, but it doesn't hurt. The doctor might ask you to take deep breaths while they listen. It's like they're using a super-powered listening tool!

instruction: Why do I have to wash my hands so much?
response: Washing your hands is one of the best things you can do at the hospital! Germs are tiny things you can't see, and they can make people sick. At the hospital, you wash your hands or use the hand sanitizer gel before going into a room, when leaving a room, and before eating. This helps stop germs from getting to you or to other kids. Think of it like being a germ-fighting superhero — every time you wash your hands, you're protecting yourself and everyone around you!

instruction: What happens when I get to the emergency room?
response: When you arrive at the Emergency Department, you and your grown-up will walk through a special doorway. There's a gentle walk-through system that checks for safety — kind of like going through an airport, but you don't have to take off your shoes or empty your pockets! Then a nurse called a triage nurse will talk to you and your family to find out what's going on and how quickly you need help. You might have to wait a little while, and that's normal. Your grown-up will stay with you the whole time.

instruction: Why can't I bring balloons to the hospital?
response: Some kinds of balloons — the stretchy ones made of latex — aren't allowed at Children's Hospital. That's because some people are really allergic to latex, and being near those balloons could make them very sick. But here's the thing — you can still bring the shiny foil balloons! Those are safe for everyone. So if someone wants to bring you a get-well balloon, just remind them to get the foil kind.

instruction: Why can't I bring perfume or smelly things?
response: Children's Hospital is a fragrance-free place. That means nobody is supposed to wear perfume, body spray, or use other strong-smelling products. This is because some patients and staff are really sensitive to smells — it can give them headaches, make it hard to breathe, or make them feel sick. So when you come to the hospital, just use unscented soap and shampoo. It helps keep the air comfortable and safe for everyone!

instruction: What is the Bravery Beads program?
response: Bravery Beads is a really special program at Children's Hospital! You get to collect beads that tell the story of everything you go through during your time at the hospital. Each bead represents something different — like a bead for getting a needle, a bead for an X-ray, or a bead for being brave during a procedure. You string them together to make your own personal necklace or collection. It's a way to remember how strong and brave you are! Any kid can join — just ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist.

instruction: Is there a clown at the hospital?
response: Yes! There's a really fun therapeutic clown named Ollie! Ollie visits kids in the hospital to bring laughter, play, and fun. A therapeutic clown is specially trained to help kids feel happy and more normal during their hospital stay. Ollie knows how to be gentle and funny in just the right way. If Ollie stops by your room, get ready for some giggles! And if you're feeling shy, that's okay too — Ollie understands.

instruction: Can a dog visit me in the hospital?
response: Children's Hospital has a special therapy dog program with dogs from St. John Ambulance. These therapy dogs are very well-trained and gentle, and they visit kids to help them feel happier and more relaxed. You can ask your nurse or care team if a therapy dog visit is coming up! Your own family pet usually can't visit, but in very special cases, the hospital might allow it with special permission. Ask your care team if you'd like to know more.

instruction: What is a Child Life Specialist?
response: A Child Life Specialist is someone whose whole job is to help kids feel better about being in the hospital! They're experts at helping kids understand what's happening, preparing you for things like tests or procedures, and helping you cope through play and fun activities. They can bring you toys, help with crafts, and explain things in ways that make sense. If you're feeling worried about something, a Child Life Specialist is a great person to talk to!

instruction: What does it feel like to get blood taken?
response: Getting blood taken means a nurse or technician will use a small needle to take a little bit of blood from your arm, usually near your elbow. But remember the Comfort Promise! They'll put numbing cream on your skin first, so you feel a lot less. You can watch a video or look at something fun while it happens. You might feel a tiny pinch or some pressure, but it's over really quickly. Afterwards, they'll put a little bandage on the spot. You did it!

instruction: What happens before an operation?
response: Before an operation, your care team will explain everything to you and your family. You might have to stop eating and drinking for a little while before — your nurse will tell you when. You'll put on a hospital gown, and the team will check your armband to make sure everything is right. Children's Hospital even has a program where your mom or dad can sometimes come into the operating room with you while you fall asleep! It's called the PPI program. Your nurse or Child Life Specialist can tell you more about it.

instruction: What does the operating room look like?
response: The operating room is a very clean, bright room with special lights above a bed in the middle. You'll see people wearing masks, caps on their heads, and special clothes. There are machines and screens around the room that help the doctors during the operation. It might look a little different from regular rooms, but everyone in there is there to help you. The team will talk to you, help you feel comfortable, and make sure you know what's happening.

instruction: What if I feel pain?
response: It's really important that you tell someone if you feel pain! The nurses and doctors at Children's Hospital really care about making sure you're comfortable. They might ask you to point to a face on a chart that shows how much it hurts — from a happy face to a really sad face. That helps them know the best way to help you. There are lots of ways they can help with pain, so always speak up. You're not being a bother — helping with pain is part of their job!

instruction: Where can I get snacks?
response: If you get hungry between meals, there are a few places to find snacks! The ward you're staying on might have a family pantry with drinks and light snacks — on the sixth floor, the pantries are in rooms B6-149 and B6-231. There are also vending machines near the elevators on the first and third floors of Zone B. And your grown-up can go to the Tim Hortons on the second floor of Zone B, which is open on weekdays from 6:30 in the morning until 8 at night. Always check with your nurse before eating, just to make sure it's okay!

instruction: What is Ashley's Backyard?
response: Ashley's Backyard is a special playroom on the sixth floor in room B6-259! It has a nature theme, so it feels like you're playing outside even though you're inside the hospital. It's designed for younger kids — babies, toddlers, and preschoolers — and their families to relax and play together. You can go there during the day and in the evening, but a grown-up needs to be with you. It's a nice break from your hospital room!

instruction: What is the activity room?
response: The School-Age Activity Room is in room B6-065 on the sixth floor, and it's full of fun things to do! You can make crafts, play board games, put puzzles together, and build with LEGO. It's open during the day from Monday to Saturday. Sometimes the Child Life staff and volunteers plan special activities and events there too! You and your family can use the room on your own, or you can join in when there's a planned activity. Just ask your nurse when it's a good time to visit.

instruction: Will someone help me if I don't understand what's happening?
response: Absolutely! You can always ask questions — any time, about anything. Your nurses, doctors, and especially the Child Life Specialists are there to explain things in a way that makes sense to you. If someone explains something and you still don't understand, it's totally okay to say 'Can you explain that differently?' Nobody will think that's silly. Your care team wants you to feel safe and know what's going on.

instruction: What is that garden outside?
response: That garden is called Alex's Butterfly Garden, and it's a beautiful, quiet outdoor space in Zone D on the second level. It has benches to sit on and a soothing water fountain. It was created for children, families, and staff to enjoy a peaceful spot for quiet memories and thinking. The garden is named in honour of babies who were very special. It's a lovely place to sit if you want some fresh air and a calm moment outside.

instruction: Why do I have to wear slip-proof socks?
response: The hospital floors can be really smooth and slippery, so wearing slip-proof socks — the kind with little grippy dots on the bottom — helps make sure you don't slide or fall. Falls can happen easily, especially if you've been lying down for a while and feel a little wobbly. Your nurse might remind you to put on your non-slip socks or slippers every time you get out of bed. It's a simple thing that helps keep you safe!

instruction: What happens during a bedside shift change?
response: A shift change is when one nurse finishes their work time and a new nurse starts. At Children's Hospital, the nurses do this right next to your bed! The new nurse will introduce themselves to you, and then the two nurses will talk about how you're doing and what the plan is for your care. They'll do some safety checks too. Your mom or dad can listen and even ask questions or share information. It takes about three to five minutes, and then your new nurse will let you know when they'll be back to check on you.

instruction: Why are the bed rails up?
response: The rails on the sides of your bed are there to keep you safe, like a little fence! When you're sleeping or resting, the rails make sure you don't accidentally roll out of bed. Your grown-up or nurse will put them up when you're lying down. When you want to get out of bed, just ask for help and someone will lower the rail for you. If you're in a crib, the sides stay up for the same reason — to keep you safe and snug!

instruction: What is a CT scan?
response: A CT scan is a special kind of picture that shows the inside of your body in really detailed slices — like slicing a loaf of bread and looking at each piece! You'll lie on a flat table that slides slowly into a big, donut-shaped machine. The machine spins around you, but you won't feel it. You just need to lie very still for a few minutes. It doesn't hurt at all! The pictures help the doctors see what's going on inside so they can take the best care of you.

instruction: What happens when I leave the hospital?
response: When it's time to go home — which is called being discharged — your care team will talk to your family about everything you need to know. They'll explain any medicines you need to take, when to come back for a check-up, and what to watch for at home. Make sure your family brings your car seat, because you need one to ride in the car! Before you leave, double-check that you've packed up all your toys and things. And don't forget to say goodbye to your nurses if you want to!

instruction: Can I play music at the hospital?
response: Children's Hospital actually has real music therapy! An accredited music therapist visits patients and uses music activities to help kids feel better. You don't need to know how to play any instruments — anyone can join in! Music therapy can help with things like feeling less pain, relaxing, and just having a good time. If you're interested, ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist if the music therapist can visit you. You can also listen to your own music on your phone or tablet with headphones.

instruction: What happens if my family speaks another language?
response: Children's Hospital has interpreters who can help! If your family is more comfortable speaking a language other than English, you can ask your care team for an interpreter — and it's totally free. The hospital knows it's really important for your family to understand everything the doctors and nurses are saying, and for the doctors to understand your family too. Just let your nurse know what language you need, and they'll arrange for help.

instruction: What does the hospital look like on the outside?
response: Children's Hospital is part of a big hospital campus at 800 Commissioners Road East in London, Ontario. It's in the area called Zone B of the Victoria Hospital site. There's a big parking garage nearby and several entrances. The main entrance to the B Tower is where most families come in. The buildings are large and connected, so once you're inside, you can walk to different areas through hallways and elevators. There are colourful signs and maps to help you find your way!

instruction: What is art therapy?
response: Art therapy is a really cool program at Children's Hospital where you get to express your feelings through art! You might draw, paint, or make things with craft supplies. A special art therapist works with you, and you don't have to be good at art — it's not about making something perfect. It's about having fun, relaxing, and letting your feelings out in a creative way. Art therapy can help you feel more in control and less stressed while you're in the hospital. Ask your care team if you'd like to try it!

instruction: What is the Sanctuary?
response: The Sanctuary is a very quiet, peaceful room where anyone can go for some calm time. It's in Zone C, on the third floor, in room C3-402. It's open all day and all night, so you can visit any time. People go there to think, pray, meditate, or just have some quiet time. It doesn't matter what religion you are or if you don't have a religion at all — everyone is welcome. If you or your family want a peaceful break, ask your nurse how to get there.

instruction: What does comfort positioning mean?
response: Comfort positioning is a way of sitting or being held during something like a needle poke that makes you feel safe and secure. Instead of lying flat and being held down, you get to sit up — maybe on your mom or dad's lap — in a big, warm hugging position. This helps you feel in control and less scared. The nurses at Children's Hospital believe this is much better than holding kids down, and research says so too! You and your family can talk to your nurse about the best comfort position for you.

instruction: What is the family lounge?
response: The Culliton Family Lounge is a comfy space on the sixth floor in room B6-110 where you can hang out with your family or friends and take a break from your hospital room. It's also used for special group events and family coffee hours. It's a nice place to relax, chat, or just spend time together in a different spot. If you're staying on the B6 inpatient unit, you're welcome to use it!

instruction: What if I can't eat before a test?
response: Sometimes before certain tests or procedures, the doctors need your tummy to be empty, so they'll ask you not to eat or drink for a little while. This is called fasting, and your nurse will tell you and your family exactly when to stop eating and when you can eat again. It can be hard to wait, especially if you're hungry, but it's really important for keeping you safe during the test. As soon as it's okay, your nurse will let you know you can eat again!

instruction: What is the Heroes' Circle?
response: The Heroes' Circle is a super cool program at Children's Hospital! It runs all year long and visits kids in the hospital every week. You get to learn breathing exercises, relaxation techniques, and even some martial arts moves! It's designed to help you feel strong, calm, and powerful. Your brothers and sisters can try it too if they're visiting. It's a fun way to learn new skills that help you feel like a hero — even while you're in the hospital!

instruction: What happens if I have an allergy?
response: If you have allergies, the hospital will make sure everyone knows about them. You'll get a special red bracelet to wear — it's different from your regular armband. This red allergy bracelet tells every single person on your care team about your allergies so they can keep you safe. Your nurses and doctors will ask you about allergies when you arrive, and they'll make sure your food and medicines are all safe for you. Always tell someone if you have allergies, even if you think they already know!

instruction: Where is the pharmacy?
response: The pharmacy at Children's Hospital is on the first floor in room B1-001, right next to the B1 entrance. It's open Monday to Friday from 8 in the morning until 5:30 in the evening. If the doctor gives you a prescription before you go home, your family can get it filled right there so you don't have to make another stop! The pharmacist there can also answer questions about your medicines.

instruction: What is the elevator like?
response: The hospital has big elevators that can fit lots of people — even people in wheelchairs or hospital beds! When you step inside, you'll see buttons for each floor. The elevators might ding when the doors open, and you might feel a little funny in your tummy when it goes up or down — like in any elevator. Near the elevators, you'll find signs and even QR codes on posters that you can scan with a phone to see a map of the hospital.

instruction: What is the quiet room for?
response: There are quiet rooms on the sixth floor — rooms B6-119 and B6-257. These are special rooms where your family can go for private talks with the care team, or where your mom or dad can take a break and have some quiet time. They can also use it to make a private phone call. These rooms aren't for sleeping, but they're perfect when someone needs a calm, private space for a little while. Just check with your nurse before using one.

instruction: What do nurses do when they first meet me?
response: When a nurse first meets you, they'll introduce themselves and tell you their name. They might look at your armband, ask you your name and birthday, and talk to your family about how you're feeling. They'll check things like your temperature, blood pressure, and heart rate. They'll also ask about any allergies and medicines you're taking. Your nurse is someone you can trust and talk to about anything — they're there to help you feel safe and taken care of!

instruction: Can I use my tablet in the hospital?
response: Yes, you can bring your own tablet, phone, or laptop to the hospital! There's WiFi you can use to go online, play games, or video chat with friends and family. The hospital also has a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free or log in to your family's streaming services. Just remember to keep the volume down so you don't disturb other kids who might be resting nearby.

instruction: What happens during a physical check-up at the hospital?
response: During a check-up, the nurse or doctor will do a few things to see how your body is doing. They'll check your temperature with a thermometer, listen to your heart and lungs with a stethoscope, check your blood pressure with the arm squeezer, and look at how much oxygen is in your blood with the finger clip. They might also look in your ears, eyes, and mouth. None of these things hurt! They're just gathering information to make sure everything is working the way it should.

instruction: What if I have to stay overnight?
response: Staying overnight at the hospital is called being an inpatient. You'll have your own bed in a room, and your mom, dad, or caregiver can stay right there with you — there's a sleeping spot for them in most rooms. You'll get meals brought to you, and the nurses will check on you during the night. You can wear your own pyjamas, have your favourite teddy with you, and even watch shows before bed. It might feel different from home, but the staff will do their best to make you comfortable.

instruction: Why does the nurse wear gloves sometimes?
response: Nurses wear gloves to protect both you and themselves from germs. The gloves are clean and new every time — they put on a fresh pair before doing things like checking your IV or helping with a bandage, and then they throw them away after. Sometimes the nurse might also wear a special gown or a mask. This is all part of keeping germs from spreading. It might look a little different, but it's a good thing!

instruction: What is a wheelchair and will I need one?
response: A wheelchair is a chair with wheels that helps people get around when walking is hard. You might use one if you're feeling tired, if your legs are sore, or if you're coming out of a procedure. There are wheelchairs at the hospital entrances, and a nurse or volunteer can help you get one. Not everyone needs a wheelchair — your care team will let you know. Getting pushed around in a wheelchair can actually be kind of fun, like a ride!

instruction: What is a cast?
response: A cast is a hard shell that goes around a broken bone to keep it still and safe while it heals. A doctor or technician will wrap your arm or leg with special materials that start soft and wet but then dry and get really hard. You might get to choose a colour! Once it's on, your bone can rest and grow back together inside. The cast might feel heavy and itchy sometimes, but you need to keep it on until the doctor says your bone is all better. Some kids get their friends to sign their cast!

instruction: What are vital signs?
response: Vital signs are measurements that show how your body is doing. The main ones are your temperature (how warm you are), your heart rate (how fast your heart is beating), your blood pressure (how hard your blood is pushing through your body), your breathing rate (how fast you're breathing), and your oxygen level (how much oxygen is in your blood). The nurse checks these regularly using tools like the thermometer, blood pressure cuff, and the little finger clip. It only takes a couple of minutes and doesn't hurt!

instruction: Will my brothers or sisters be able to visit me?
response: Your brothers and sisters can come visit you! Children's Hospital wants you to have the support of your family and friends. Visitors should check with the unit staff about the best times to visit. Everyone who visits should wash their hands or use hand sanitizer when they arrive. The hospital asks that nobody visits if they're feeling sick. During nighttime hours between 8 p.m. and 8 a.m., visitors should stay in your room and let the staff know they're there.

instruction: What does it mean when they say Zone B?
response: The hospital is divided into different sections called zones, and each one has a letter. Children's Hospital is in Zone B! When you see a room number like B6-065, the B tells you it's in Zone B, the 6 tells you it's on the sixth floor, and 065 is the room number. Other parts of the bigger Victoria Hospital are in zones like C, D, and E. Knowing your zone and floor is like having a treasure map code that helps you find your way around!

instruction: What is the Information Desk?
response: The Information Desk is a spot where friendly staff and volunteers can help you and your family find your way around the hospital, answer questions, and point you in the right direction. The desks are open from 8 in the morning to 8 at night on weekdays, and from noon to 4 in the afternoon on weekends. There are also guide volunteers near the B1 entrance and B2 lobby on weekdays until 3 p.m. If you're ever not sure where to go, these are great people to ask!

instruction: What does it smell like when they clean my skin before a needle?
response: Before a needle, the nurse might wipe your skin with a little wet pad that smells like rubbing alcohol. It's a sharp, clean smell that goes away pretty quickly. The wipe might feel cool on your skin for a second. This cleaning step gets rid of any germs on your skin before the needle goes in. If they're using the Comfort Promise numbing cream, that goes on first and doesn't have much of a smell at all.

instruction: What is a family pantry?
response: The family pantry is a small room on the ward where your family can find drinks and light snacks. On the sixth floor, the pantries are in rooms B6-149 and B6-231. There's also a family fridge with a freezer where your family can store their own food — just make sure everything is labeled with your name and the date. It's a handy spot so your family doesn't always have to leave the floor to grab something to eat or drink!

instruction: What does the MazeMap app do?
response: MazeMap is a really cool map app that works like GPS but for inside the hospital! Your family can download it on a phone and search for the Victoria Hospital map. It shows you where everything is — rooms, elevators, washrooms, cafeterias, and more. You can also find maps on special screens called wayfinding kiosks around the hospital, or scan QR codes on posters near the elevators. It's super helpful for finding your way around this big place!

instruction: What is a red allergy bracelet?
response: A red allergy bracelet is a special wristband you wear in addition to your regular hospital armband if you have any allergies. It's bright red so that every single person on your care team can easily see it and remember your allergies. This way, before anyone gives you food or medicine, they'll check your red bracelet and make sure it's safe for you. It's another way the hospital keeps you protected!

instruction: Can I do crafts at the hospital?
response: Yes! The School-Age Activity Room on the sixth floor (room B6-065) has all kinds of crafts for you. You might get to paint, make things with paper, build with LEGO, or do other creative projects. The Child Life staff and volunteers plan special craft activities throughout the month. You can also do art therapy with a real art therapist! And you're welcome to bring your own colouring books, crayons, or craft supplies from home too.

instruction: What are the food options for my parents?
response: Your parents can get food at a Tim Hortons spot called 'On the Go' on the second floor of Zone B — it's open on weekdays from 6:30 in the morning until 8 at night, but it's closed on weekends and holidays. There are also vending machines near the elevators on the first and third floors of Zone B. And if your family brings their own food, they can store it in the family fridge in the pantry rooms. Just remember to label everything with your name and the date!

instruction: What does it feel like to ride in a hospital bed?
response: If you need to go somewhere in the hospital, sometimes the nurses will wheel your whole bed there! The bed has wheels on the bottom, and it feels a little like a slow ride. You might see the ceiling tiles going by above you and hear the wheels rolling on the floor. The nurses will guide the bed carefully through hallways and into elevators. It might feel different, but you'll be safe the whole time, and you can bring your stuffed animal along for the ride!

instruction: What is a waiting room like?
response: A waiting room is a big room with chairs where families sit and wait until it's their turn to see the doctor or have a test done. You might see other kids and families there too. There are usually things to look at or read, and you can bring your own books, toys, or a tablet to keep busy. Sometimes the wait can feel long, but your grown-up will be right there with you. When it's your turn, someone will call your name and take you to where you need to go.

instruction: What is an MRI?
response: An MRI is a machine that takes really detailed pictures of the inside of your body. It's a big tube-shaped machine, and you lie on a flat bed that slides inside it. The machine makes loud knocking and buzzing sounds — kind of like a drum beat! They'll give you special headphones or ear plugs so the noise isn't too loud. The most important thing is to lie really still, like a statue. It doesn't hurt at all, but it might feel a little strange being in a small space. Your family will be nearby the whole time.

instruction: Why do some people wear masks in the hospital?
response: Some people at the hospital wear masks over their nose and mouth to help stop germs from spreading. This is especially important for protecting patients who are already sick and might catch germs more easily. The hospital has masks at all the entrances for anyone who wants to wear one. If you're visiting someone who needs extra germ protection, you might be asked to put one on too. It can feel a little funny, but it's a really kind way to keep everyone safe!

instruction: What happens if I feel dizzy after a procedure?
response: Feeling a little dizzy or woozy after a procedure is normal for some kids. Your nurse knows this might happen and will keep a close eye on you. They'll make sure you stay in bed until you feel steady, and the bed rails will be up to keep you safe. If you feel dizzy, tell your nurse right away — you don't have to be brave about it! They can help you feel better. Drinking water and resting usually helps the dizziness go away.

instruction: What do I do if the machines start beeping a lot?
response: If the machines near your bed start beeping more than usual, don't worry! Often the beeping just means something small happened — like the clip on your finger moved or a tube shifted a tiny bit. A nurse will come check on it. You don't have to fix anything yourself. If a nurse doesn't come right away, you can press your call button and let them know. The machines are there to help, and the beeping is their way of telling the nurses to come take a look.

instruction: Why do they have hand sanitizer at every door?
response: There are hand sanitizer dispensers at every door because clean hands are the number one way to stop germs from spreading in the hospital! Every person — doctors, nurses, visitors, and kids — should clean their hands when going in and out of rooms. The hospital uses alcohol-based hand rub, and it only takes about 20 seconds to rub it all over your hands. Think of each dispenser as a tiny germ-fighting station, and you're the hero who uses it!

instruction: What happens when the nurse takes my temperature with an ear thermometer?
response: The nurse will gently put a small probe into your ear — it doesn't go in very far, just a tiny bit. You'll hear a little beep after a second or two, and that's it! The thermometer reads how warm you are from inside your ear. It doesn't hurt, but it might feel a little tickly. Each time the nurse uses it, they put a brand new clean cover on the tip. It's one of the quickest check-ups the nurse does!

instruction: What do I do at the hospital if I get bored?
response: There are lots of things to do if you get bored! You can visit the activity rooms on the sixth floor for crafts and games, try the SMILE Room with its cool lights and music, ask about art therapy or music therapy, or see if Ollie the Clown is visiting. You can also bring your own toys, books, colouring supplies, or a tablet from home. There's free TV and you can use your family's streaming services. And the Heroes' Circle program teaches fun breathing and martial arts moves!

instruction: Why does my bed go up and down?
response: Hospital beds are really special because they have a motor inside that lets them move! The nurses can raise or lower different parts of the bed using buttons. They might raise the head part so you can sit up to eat or watch TV, or raise the whole bed so it's easier for the nurse to take care of you. Sometimes your nurse might let you try the buttons yourself. It's like having a recliner that can do way more tricks!

instruction: What's it like to have stitches?
response: If you need stitches, a doctor will use a special needle and thread to close up a cut so it can heal properly. Before they start, they'll numb the area so you don't feel the stitching — you might feel some pressure or tugging, but not sharp pain. The stitches look like tiny loops of thread in your skin. After a while, when the cut has healed, you'll come back or a nurse will take them out. Some stitches even dissolve on their own! If you're nervous about it, tell your care team and they can help you feel more comfortable.

instruction: What happens during a hearing test?
response: During a hearing test, you'll usually sit in a special quiet room or wear headphones. A technician will play different sounds — some soft and some louder, some high and some low — and you'll raise your hand or press a button when you hear them. It doesn't hurt at all! It's kind of like a game of 'can you hear this?' The test helps the doctors make sure your ears are working well. If you're not sure what to do, the technician will explain everything before you start.

instruction: What is a nebulizer?
response: A nebulizer is a machine that turns liquid medicine into a fine mist so you can breathe it right into your lungs. You wear a little mask over your nose and mouth, or sometimes just use a mouthpiece, and breathe normally while the mist comes out. The machine makes a quiet humming sound, and the mist might feel cool or wet on your face. It doesn't hurt at all! You just sit and breathe for about 10 to 15 minutes while the medicine goes in. You can watch TV or read a book while it's working.

instruction: What is the Paediatric Family Resource Centre?
response: The Paediatric Family Resource Centre is a special room on the first floor of Zone B, in room B1-006. It's a quiet place where you and your family can find information about different health topics, use the internet, and get help and support from friendly people who understand what it's like to have a kid in the hospital. It's open most days of the week, and on Saturdays and Sundays by appointment. If you or your family need a calm place to take a break or look something up, it's a great spot to visit!

instruction: What should I expect when I arrive at Children's Hospital for the first time?
response: When you arrive at Children's Hospital, you'll enter through the B Tower main entrance at 800 Commissioners Road East in London. The entrance is open from 6:00 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. daily — after that, Security controls access. Head up to the second floor of Zone B for Patient Registration, where you'll check in with your health card and appointment details. You'll be given an identification armband with your name, date of birth, hospital ID number, and a barcode. Staff will scan this band before any procedure, test, or medication, so expect to be asked to confirm your name and date of birth frequently. It's a standard safety protocol, not a sign that anything's wrong.

instruction: What does the identification armband do?
response: Your ID armband is a critical safety tool. It contains your full name, date of birth, a unique hospital ID number, and a scannable barcode. Before any medication, test, procedure, or transport, a member of your care team will scan or visually check your armband to confirm your identity. You'll also be verbally asked to confirm your name and birthday — sometimes multiple times a day. It might feel repetitive, but it's a core patient safety practice designed to prevent errors. If you have known allergies, you'll also receive a separate red allergy bracelet so every staff member is immediately aware.

instruction: How does the hospital's Comfort Promise work for teens?
response: The Comfort Promise is Children's Hospital's commitment to minimizing pain and anxiety during needle procedures, and it applies to patients of all ages, including teens. Evidence-based strategies include topical anesthetic (a numbing cream or gel applied to the skin before a needle), comfort positioning (sitting upright in a supportive position rather than being restrained), and distraction (watching something on your phone, listening to music, or any activity that redirects your focus). Research shows that untreated needle pain can lead to long-term effects like healthcare avoidance, increased pain sensitivity, and even vaccine hesitancy. You have every right to ask for these comfort measures — it's not just for younger kids.

instruction: What are the visiting hours and rules?
response: Visiting at Children's Hospital is flexible and based on each patient's condition and care needs, so there aren't rigid universal hours. However, there are some consistent guidelines. You're allowed up to two care partners at the bedside at one time for inpatients, or one for outpatient visits. Between 8:00 p.m. and 8:00 a.m., anyone staying with you should remain in your room and let unit staff know when they arrive and leave. All visitors should wash their hands or use hand sanitizer before and after visiting, and anyone who's been sick in the past week should stay home. Specific units may have additional restrictions, so check with staff on your unit for the details.

instruction: What is the weapons detection system in the Emergency Department?
response: When you enter the Emergency Department at Children's Hospital, you'll pass through a weapons detection system. It uses advanced, non-invasive technology — you just walk through without stopping or emptying your pockets. It's designed to maintain a safe environment for everyone. If the system flags something, a trained security guard may check your belongings. If you need specific accommodations, you can speak to the security guard at the ED entrance before going through. The system scans everyone, including minors accompanied by a parent or guardian.

instruction: How do room numbers work?
response: Room numbers at Children's Hospital follow a consistent format that's actually pretty straightforward once you know the code. A room number like B2-503 breaks down as: B = Zone B (the zone of the hospital), 2 = second floor, and 503 = the specific room number. Children's Hospital is in Zone B of the Victoria Hospital campus. Knowing this system helps you navigate independently. You can also download the MazeMap app for an interactive indoor map, use wayfinding kiosks on-site, or scan QR codes on posters near elevator bays.

instruction: What does it feel like to get an IV?
response: Having an IV placed involves a needle puncture into a vein, typically in your hand or forearm. You'll feel a pinch or prick when the needle goes in, but the Comfort Promise means your care team will offer topical anesthetic to numb the area first, and you can use distraction techniques like listening to music or watching something on your phone. Once the IV catheter is in place, the needle is actually removed — what stays in your vein is a thin, flexible plastic tube. The tube is secured with tape or a clear dressing. After placement, you might feel mild pressure at the site, but it shouldn't be painful. If it starts hurting, feels swollen, or looks red, tell your nurse immediately.

instruction: Where can I get food at the hospital?
response: If you're admitted, patient meals are served at set times: breakfast from 7:45 to 8:45 a.m., lunch from 11:45 a.m. to 12:45 p.m., and dinner from 4:45 to 5:45 p.m. You'll get a menu card on your breakfast tray to select your next day's meals. The hospital accommodates a range of dietary needs including vegan, vegetarian, halal, kosher, and specific allergen restrictions — just let your care team know. For snacks between meals, the inpatient unit on B6 has pantries in rooms B6-149 and B6-231 with drinks and light snacks. There's also a Tim Hortons ('On the Go') on the second floor of Zone B, open weekdays from 6:30 a.m. to 8:00 p.m., and vending machines near the Zone B elevators on the first and third floors. Always check with your care team before eating, as some tests or procedures require fasting.

instruction: Can I use my phone and access WiFi at the hospital?
response: Yes. The hospital supports and encourages patients to use their own cell phones. There's WiFi available, and the hospital provides a patient entertainment site where you can watch live Rogers TV for free or log in to your own streaming services. Patient telephones in your room can also be used for local and toll-free calls at no charge. If you run into any issues with WiFi connectivity, you can call the Data Valet/WiFi support line at 1-800-642-3958.

instruction: What should I bring for a hospital stay?
response: For your stay, you'll want to bring your Ontario health card, any appointment letters, a list of your current medications (including over-the-counter and herbal supplements), and your family doctor's contact info. For personal comfort, pack your own clothes including sleepwear and slippers, toiletries, and any medical aids like glasses or braces. You can bring a few comfort items — books, a tablet, headphones, family photos — but keep it manageable since clutter can interfere with care delivery and cleaning. Toys and items should be clean and ideally wipeable. Don't bring latex balloons, perfume or fragranced products, electrical equipment, or baby walkers. Keep valuables to a minimum and bring a small amount of cash for vending machines or snacks.

instruction: What is the bedside shift change?
response: At Children's Hospital, nursing shift changes happen at your bedside rather than behind closed doors. Shifts change around 6:45 to 7:30 a.m. and 6:45 to 7:30 p.m. During this handover, the incoming nurse will introduce themselves, both nurses will review your care plan and complete mandatory safety checks, and you'll have a chance to ask questions or share anything you think is important. The whole process takes about three to five minutes. You and your family are encouraged to participate — it's a direct way to stay informed about your care and ensure nothing gets lost in translation between shifts.

instruction: What does it mean to be on a locked unit?
response: The B6 inpatient unit is a locked unit, which means doors are secured and access is controlled. Once you're admitted, you'll be given a confidential code to get in and out. This isn't about restricting you — it's a security measure to protect all patients on the floor, especially younger children. One family member can stay overnight with you. Clean sheets, pillows, and blankets are provided for the sleep space. If you feel uncomfortable with the locked setup, talk to your care team about any concerns.

instruction: What happens during an MRI?
response: An MRI uses powerful magnets and radio waves to create detailed images of your body's internal structures — no radiation involved. You'll lie on a narrow table that slides into a large tube-shaped scanner. The machine produces loud rhythmic knocking and humming sounds, so you'll be given ear protection. The key requirement is staying completely still for the duration of the scan, which can range from 20 minutes to over an hour depending on what's being imaged. The space inside the scanner is fairly tight, which can feel claustrophobic for some people — let your care team know beforehand if that's a concern. You won't feel any pain during the scan itself.

instruction: What is a CT scan like?
response: A CT scan uses X-ray technology to create cross-sectional images of your body. You lie flat on a motorized table that slides through a large, donut-shaped ring. The ring rotates around you while capturing images — you won't feel anything from the scan itself. You'll need to stay still, and you might be asked to briefly hold your breath. In some cases, you may receive contrast dye through an IV, which can cause a warm or flushed feeling and a metallic taste — that's temporary and normal. The whole process is usually quick, often under 15 minutes. The detailed images help your care team assess internal structures that standard X-rays can't capture as clearly.

instruction: How does the hospital protect my privacy?
response: At LHSC, your health information can only be shared with your parent(s) or legal guardian(s). You have specific rights regarding your personal health information, including the right to consent to or refuse how it's collected, used, and disclosed, the right to access it, and the right to be notified if it's accessed inappropriately. During your stay, your family might consider designating one contact person who can relay updates to extended family, so the care team isn't sharing information repeatedly. If you want to call the unit to check on something, provide the patient's full name and ask for their nurse. Just be aware that calls during nursing shift changes (6:45–7:30 a.m. and 6:45–7:30 p.m.) may be harder to get through.

instruction: What infection prevention protocols should I be aware of?
response: Hand hygiene is the top priority. Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) dispensers are located throughout the hospital, and you should clean your hands before entering a patient room, when leaving, and at the end of any visit. If a patient requires additional infection control precautions, you'll see a sign posted at the room or bed space entry. This might mean wearing gloves, a gown, a mask, or eye protection — staff will walk you through it. Other practical rules: don't visit if you're sick, don't sit on hospital beds or put feet on bedded chairs, don't use patient washrooms if you're a visitor, and don't touch supplies on carts — ask staff instead. Keeping personal items minimal also helps the cleaning team maintain hygiene.

instruction: What is the Paediatric Critical Care Unit (PCCU) like?
response: The PCCU is the intensive care unit for paediatric patients. It has higher nurse-to-patient ratios and more advanced monitoring equipment than a general ward. At the bedside, there are two sleep spaces available for family members, with clean sheets, pillows, and blankets provided. There's also a nearby quiet room that sleeps one and a sleep room that sleeps two — both share a bathroom with a shower. Expect to see more machines and monitors than in a regular room, and more frequent check-ins from the care team. The environment can feel intense, but the staff are specialists in critical care for children and teens.

instruction: What is Upopolis?
response: Upopolis is a free, secure social networking platform specifically for paediatric patients ages 8 to 18. It lets you connect with other young patients across Canada who are going through similar experiences. You can access it through laptops available from Child Life Services. It's a way to find peer support and feel less isolated during your hospital stay. If you're interested, speak with a Child Life Specialist on your unit and they can help you get set up.

instruction: What are the SMILE Room and other special spaces?
response: The SMILE Room (B6-261) is a sensory room equipped with bubble columns, fibre optics, mirrors, and music, designed to help with relaxation or stimulation depending on what you need. Beyond that, there's Ashley's Backyard (B6-259), a nature-themed playroom primarily for younger patients; the School-Age Activity Room (B6-065) with crafts, board games, and LEGO; the Culliton Family Lounge (B6-110) for socializing; quiet rooms in B6-119 and B6-257 for private conversations or a break; and the Sanctuary (C3-402), a 24/7 sacred space open to everyone for prayer, meditation, or quiet reflection. There's also Alex's Butterfly Garden in Zone D on Level 2 — an outdoor space with benches and a water fountain.

instruction: What is the Parental Presence at Anaesthesia Induction (PPI) program?
response: The PPI program at Children's Hospital prepares one caregiver to accompany you into the operating room during the initial stage of anaesthesia — when you're being put to sleep. Before the procedure, the program offers an education session and/or a tour of Day Surgery and the OR so both you and your caregiver know what to expect. Having a familiar person present during induction can significantly reduce anxiety. Not every patient is eligible for PPI, so discuss it with your care team or a Child Life Specialist to find out if it's an option for your procedure.

instruction: How does fall prevention work here?
response: When you're admitted, your nurse will do a fall risk assessment and go over fall prevention strategies with you and your family. Even if you're usually steady on your feet, being in a hospital — with unfamiliar surroundings, medications that might make you drowsy, and periods of bed rest — can increase fall risk. Practical steps include wearing slip-proof socks or slippers whenever you get up, keeping bed rails raised when you're in bed, keeping the floor clear of clutter, and asking for help before getting out of bed if you've been sedated or feel unsteady. If any staff leave items that create a trip hazard, flag it.

instruction: What should I expect with blood draws?
response: A blood draw (venipuncture) involves a phlebotomist or nurse inserting a needle into a vein, usually at the inside of your elbow or on the back of your hand, to collect blood samples for lab testing. Under the Comfort Promise, you can request topical anesthetic to numb the site beforehand. The needle insertion feels like a quick pinch — most of the discomfort is over in a couple of seconds. Distraction techniques like music, conversation, or looking at your phone can help. After the draw, they'll apply a small bandage. Mild bruising at the site is normal and resolves within a few days. If you're someone who's had bad experiences with needles in the past, tell your care team — they can plan extra comfort measures.

instruction: What does the hospital smell like and why?
response: Hospitals have a distinctive smell that mostly comes from cleaning agents and alcohol-based hand sanitizer used to maintain sterile environments. You might also pick up the scent of medical supplies and adhesives. LHSC is a fragrance-free facility, which means staff, patients, and visitors are asked not to wear perfume, cologne, or scented products — this is to prevent allergic reactions and respiratory issues for sensitive patients. So the overall scent profile is clinical rather than pleasant, but it's a sign that infection control is being taken seriously.

instruction: What services are available to help me cope emotionally?
response: Children's Hospital has several programs designed to support your emotional wellbeing. Child Life Specialists help with preparation for procedures and coping strategies. The Art Therapy program lets you express thoughts and feelings through creative activities. Music Therapy, led by an accredited therapist, supports areas like pain control, relaxation, and rehabilitation — no musical skill required. The Heroes' Circle teaches breathing, relaxation, and martial arts techniques. Paediatric Psychology Services offer assessment and treatment for challenges in adjusting to illness, plus coping strategies for managing symptoms. And if you want to connect with peers, Upopolis is a secure online network for patients ages 8–18. If you're struggling, let your care team know — they can connect you with the right support.

instruction: What does an X-ray involve?
response: An X-ray is a quick imaging test that uses a small amount of radiation to produce images of internal structures, most commonly bones. You'll be positioned by a radiologic technologist — standing, sitting, or lying down depending on what's being imaged. A lead apron may be placed over parts of your body that don't need to be scanned to minimize radiation exposure. The machine makes a brief click or buzzing sound when the image is captured. The entire process is usually done in minutes. It's painless, though holding a specific position can be mildly uncomfortable if you're injured. X-ray results typically get reviewed by your care team quickly.

instruction: What happens before surgery?
response: Before surgery, your care team will explain the procedure, risks, benefits, and what to expect for recovery. You'll likely need to fast for a specific period beforehand — your nurse will give you exact instructions on when to stop eating and drinking. On the day of surgery, you'll change into a hospital gown, and staff will confirm your identity using your armband multiple times. Your vitals will be checked, and you'll meet the anaesthesia team. If you're eligible for the PPI program, one caregiver can accompany you into the OR during anaesthesia induction. A Child Life Specialist can also help with preparation if you're anxious. After surgery, you'll be monitored in a recovery area before returning to your room.

instruction: What does an ultrasound feel like?
response: An ultrasound uses high-frequency sound waves to create real-time images of internal organs and structures. A technician applies warm gel to your skin over the area being examined, then moves a handheld probe (called a transducer) across the gel. The probe sends sound waves into your body that bounce back to create images on a screen. You won't feel the sound waves — just the pressure of the probe and the slipperiness of the gel. It's completely painless and doesn't involve any radiation. The gel gets wiped off afterward. Depending on the area, you may be asked to fast or drink extra water beforehand to improve image quality.

instruction: What should I expect from the Paediatric Emergency Department?
response: When you arrive at the Paediatric ED, you'll pass through the weapons detection system at the entrance — it's quick and non-invasive. You'll then be seen by a triage nurse who will assess your symptoms and assign a priority level. Depending on the severity, you may be seen immediately or have a wait. One caregiver is expected to stay with you at all times. There are no sleeping accommodations in the ED, but staff will try to provide a reclining or fold-out chair with pillows and blankets. The environment can be busy and noisy, with lots of activity. Bring something to pass the time — your phone, headphones, a book. If your condition changes while waiting, let staff know immediately.

instruction: How does the Bravery Beads program work?
response: Bravery Beads is a voluntary program open to patients of all ages who are dealing with a long-term or chronic illness or injury. Each bead represents a specific element of your care or treatment — procedures, tests, milestones in your journey. You string them together to create a tangible record of what you've been through. It's a way to acknowledge and document your experience, and many patients find it empowering to see their resilience represented physically. Ask your nurse or a Child Life Specialist if you'd like to participate.

instruction: What does an overnight stay look like?
response: If you're admitted as an inpatient, you'll be assigned a room on the ward. Your bed has adjustable positioning and side rails. One family member can stay overnight — a sleep space with clean linens is provided in most rooms. Nurses will check on you regularly throughout the night to monitor your safety and comfort. Meals are served at set times, and you can use the family pantry for snacks. You can wear your own clothes, use your phone, watch TV, and access streaming services. During nighttime hours (8 p.m. to 8 a.m.), visitors should remain in the room. You'll sleep in your own hospital bed — no doubling up — so nurses can access you easily.

instruction: How do I navigate the hospital?
response: Children's Hospital is in Zone B of the Victoria Hospital campus. Zones are labeled with letters (B, C, D, E), and room numbers encode the zone, floor, and room — like B6-261 means Zone B, sixth floor, room 261. For wayfinding, you have several options: download the MazeMap app and search for the Victoria Hospital map, use wayfinding kiosks located throughout the building, or scan QR codes on posters near elevator bays. Information Desks are staffed 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. on weekdays and noon to 4:00 p.m. on weekends. Guide volunteers are at the B1 entrance and B2 lobby from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. on weekdays.

instruction: What are vital signs and how are they measured?
response: Vital signs are routine measurements that give your care team a snapshot of your basic body functions. They include: temperature (measured with an oral, ear, or forehead thermometer), heart rate (pulse, often measured via a monitor or manually), blood pressure (using an inflatable cuff that temporarily squeezes your arm), respiratory rate (counting your breaths per minute), and oxygen saturation (measured with a pulse oximeter clipped to your finger, which uses a light sensor to measure blood oxygen levels). These checks are done frequently — sometimes every few hours — and are completely painless. Changes in vital signs help your care team detect issues early.

instruction: What is a pulse oximeter?
response: A pulse oximeter is a small, clip-like device placed on your fingertip. It shines infrared and red light through your skin to measure the oxygen saturation of your blood — essentially, how well your body is transporting oxygen. It also reads your pulse rate. The clip feels like a gentle clothespin and doesn't cause any pain. You'll see a number displayed on a monitor, usually between 95 and 100 percent for healthy levels. If the reading drops or fluctuates, it might trigger an alarm on the monitor — often it's just because the clip shifted. Your nurse will check and reposition it if needed.

instruction: What sounds should I expect in the hospital?
response: Hospitals have a distinct soundscape. Monitors produce steady beeping that corresponds to heart rates and oxygen levels. Infusion pumps attached to IVs make periodic sounds, especially when a bag is running low or there's an occlusion. You'll hear overhead announcements, doors opening and closing, footsteps in the hallway, and occasional alarms. In units like the PCCU, the density of monitoring equipment means the ambient beeping is more constant. At night, the hospital quiets down but doesn't go silent — nurses still move through the halls and check on patients. If any alarm sound worries you, ask your nurse what it means.

instruction: What is the fragrance-free policy?
response: LHSC maintains a fragrance-free environment across all its facilities. This means patients, visitors, and staff are asked not to use or bring any scented products — perfume, cologne, body spray, scented lotions, or other fragranced items. The reason is medical: fragrances can trigger allergic reactions, migraines, and respiratory distress in sensitive individuals, including immunocompromised patients. Use unscented versions of personal care products during your stay and remind anyone who plans to visit to do the same.

instruction: Why can't I bring latex balloons?
response: Latex balloons are banned throughout LHSC due to latex allergy risk. Latex allergies can cause severe reactions including anaphylaxis in sensitized individuals, and in a hospital where immunocompromised and allergic patients are nearby, this is a serious concern. Foil (mylar) balloons are a safe alternative. Similarly, poinsettia plants are prohibited because they contain a compound chemically similar to rubber latex that can trigger reactions through touch or inhalation.

instruction: What is the parking situation?
response: The closest lot to Children's Hospital is Parking Lot P8, a parking garage off Baseline Road near the northwest corner of the campus. When entering, take a ticket from the gate machine. Rates are $4 for the first hour, $2 for each additional half hour, up to a daily max of $12 (no in-and-out privileges at the standard rate). You can pay at automated stations near the second-floor elevators in the P8 garage. For longer stays, passes with in-and-out privileges are available from the parking office (P8, ground floor, room 105, open Monday–Friday 8 a.m.–8 p.m.): 7-day for $45, 14-day for $65, or 30-day for $75. All passes are valid across LHSC sites for one year from purchase.

instruction: What does the pre-op fasting process involve?
response: Before certain procedures and surgeries, you'll be required to fast — meaning no food or drink for a specified period. Your care team will give you specific instructions about when to stop eating and drinking. The purpose is to ensure your stomach is empty, which reduces the risk of aspiration (food or liquid entering your lungs) during anaesthesia. The fasting window varies depending on the procedure and the type of anaesthesia being used. It can be uncomfortable, especially if you're already anxious, but it's an essential safety precaution. Once your procedure is complete and your care team clears you, you'll be able to eat and drink again.

instruction: What can I expect from the discharge process?
response: Discharge planning starts early in your admission. Before you leave, your care team will go over your care instructions, including medications (purpose, dosage, timing, side effects), dietary needs, activity restrictions, and follow-up appointments. You'll receive written instructions to take home. Make sure you understand everything — ask for clarification if anything's unclear. Your family should bring a car seat if required by law (all children legally need one). If your stay was longer than 14 days or you need home care services, a referral to Ontario Health atHome may be needed. Try to be ready to leave at your scheduled discharge time, though it may shift. If transportation is an issue, ask your nurse about options.

instruction: What does the monitor next to my bed track?
response: The bedside monitor typically tracks several vital parameters in real time. The most common readings are your heart rate (displayed as a waveform and a number), oxygen saturation via a pulse oximeter, blood pressure (taken at intervals through an automated cuff), and respiratory rate. Some monitors also display temperature and cardiac rhythm. Each parameter has a set alarm range — if a reading falls outside that range, the monitor will beep.
